Brouwer fixed-point theorem (F(x∗​)=x∗​)

Words: 1k Articles: 9
Topological analysis OurBigBook.com
The Brouwer fixed-point theorem says that every continuous map F:K→K has a fixed point when K is a nonempty compact set and a convex set in a finite-dimensional vector space over the real numbers. Equivalently, take K⊆Rn for a finite n, with the usual Euclidean space structure: there is some x∗​∈K such that F(x∗​)=x∗​. The conclusion guarantees at least one fixed point, without asserting uniqueness or telling us how quickly to find one. [ref]
The standard pictures are a closed ball, including a closed unit ball, and a simplex. A filled disk qualifies; its bounding circle alone does not. A probability simplex also qualifies even though its dimension is smaller than that of its ambient Euclidean space. The hypotheses have concrete meanings: being a convex set keeps every line segment between allowed points inside K, and compactness prevents escape or loss of a limiting point. In Euclidean space, the Heine-Borel theorem identifies compact sets with closed sets that are bounded sets. Crucially, every output must belong to the same K as the input.
For a fully computable example, let D={(u,v):u2+v2≤1} be the filled unit disk. Apply a counterclockwise quarter-turn rotation, shrink by 0.4, and add a translation:
R90​(u,v)=(−v,u),F(u,v)=0.4R90​(u,v)+(0.3,0.1).
(1)
This affine map is a continuous map. Because the rotation preserves the Euclidean norm, the triangle inequality gives, for every x∈D,
∥F(x)∥≤0.4∥x∥+∥(0.3,0.1)∥≤0.4+0.1​≈0.716228<1.
(2)
Thus the whole image lies strictly inside D. More precisely, it is a disk of radius 0.4 centred at (0.3,0.1). This containment check is what makes the Brouwer fixed-point theorem applicable; a formula being a continuous map by itself would not suffice.
The fixed point can now be found by a system of linear equations:
u=−52​v+103​,v=52​u+101​,x∗​=(5813​,5811​)≈(0.224138,0.189655).
(3)
Indeed, substitution gives F(x∗​)=(−22/290+87/290,26/290+29/290)=x∗​. Its Euclidean norm is 290​/58≈0.293610, safely inside D. The figure shows arrows from sample inputs to their outputs; an arrow disappears at the fixed point because the displacement F(x)−x vanishes there.
Repeated iterations of a map happen to succeed for this example. Starting at x0​=(1,0) and setting xk+1​=F(xk​) gives x1​=(0.3,0.5), x2​=(0.1,0.22), and x3​=(0.212,0.14). Subtracting the fixed point equation yields xk+1​−x∗​=0.4R90​(xk​−x∗​), so the Euclidean distance to x∗​ shrinks by exactly 0.4 each step. This extra fact follows from the contraction mapping property and the Banach fixed-point theorem. It is additional information beyond the Brouwer fixed-point theorem.
The distinction becomes visible with two simpler continuous maps of the same disk. The pure rotation G(u,v)=(−v,u) has exactly one fixed point, (0,0), since u=−v and v=u force both to vanish. Yet iterations of a map starting at (1,0) here cycle through (0,1), (−1,0), and (0,−1) forever. Their Euclidean distance from (0,0) stays one, so there is no convergence in a metric space. The reflection H(u,v)=(u,−v) has an entire line segment of fixed points, namely {(u,0):−1≤u≤1}. Starting off that line segment produces an alternating pair. Existence, uniqueness, and convergence of iterations of a map are separate questions.
Removing hypotheses changes the answer. Restrict the same quarter-turn rotation to the circle S1={(u,v):u2+v2=1}. It remains a continuous map into that compact set, but its only possible fixed point, (0,0), has been removed. The circle is not a convex set. Conversely, on the unbounded convex set R, the translation t↦t+1 has no fixed point; on the open interval (0,1), t↦(t+1)/2 also has none. Neither domain is a compact set. The finite-dimensional closed ball statement should likewise not be extended to arbitrary infinite-dimensional vector spaces, where a closed ball need not be a compact set.
The one-dimensional version explains the connection to the intermediate value theorem. For a continuous map f:[a,b]→[a,b], put h(t)=f(t)−t. Then h(a)≥0 and h(b)≤0, so the intermediate value theorem gives h(c)=0 for some c∈[a,b]. In higher dimensions, the Brouwer fixed-point theorem supplies a corresponding existence principle when this scalar sign argument is unavailable. Its practical value is ensuring that a proposed equation x=F(x) has a solution once a suitable domain is found; it supplies no general promise of a fast algorithm.
A useful application is positive matrix eigenvector from simplex normalization: rescale the output of a strictly positive matrix to make its entries sum to one. For example, take
A=(21​12​),x=(t,1−t),0≤t≤1.
(4)
On this probability simplex, Ax=(1+t,2−t) has entry sum 3, so the normalized continuous map is T(x)=((1+t)/3,(2−t)/3). Both entries are positive and sum to one, keeping the image inside the probability simplex. Its fixed point equation is t=(1+t)/3, hence t=1/2. Consequently x∗​=(1/2,1/2) satisfies Ax∗​=(3/2,3/2)=3x∗​: a strictly positive eigenvector with eigenvalue 3. In larger dimensions, the Brouwer fixed-point theorem guarantees the corresponding positive eigenvector without requiring us to solve a system of linear equations in advance. The fixed point expresses preservation of relative weights, rather than preservation of their unnormalized size.
Proofs can be approached through the no-retraction theorem or Sperner's lemma. In the latter approach, increasingly fine triangulations locate approximate fixed points; compactness supplies a convergent subsequence, and continuous maps turn its limit into an exact fixed point. [ref]
A primary historical reference is L. E. J. Brouwer's 1911 paper Über Abbildung von Mannigfaltigkeiten, whose digitized original is hosted by Zenodo under DOI 10.1007/BF01456812. This gives a direct route to the early literature behind the Brouwer fixed-point theorem. [ref]

Invariant ball from sublinear growth (∣f(x)∣≤A∣x∣α+B,0<α<1)

Words: 54
Brouwer fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
A continuous Euclidean self-map with this growth has a fixed point. Choose R≥(2A)1/(1−α) and R≥2B. Then ∣f(x)∣≤R whenever ∣x∣≤R, so the closed radius-R ball is invariant and Brouwer applies. Existence does not imply convergence of iterating the original map: x↦1−x on the unit interval has a fixed point but a two-cycle from either endpoint.

Outward vector field zero theorem (g(x)⋅x≥0 on ∣x∣=R ⟹ ∃∣x0​∣≤R:g(x0​)=0)

Words: 59
Brouwer fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
A continuous vector field on a closed Euclidean ball whose boundary values have nonnegative outward component has a zero in the ball. Otherwise T(x)=−Rg(x)/∣g(x)∣ is a continuous self-map of the ball. Its fixed point, supplied by the Brouwer fixed-point theorem, lies on the boundary and satisfies g(x)⋅x=−R∣g(x)∣<0, a contradiction. The argument turns a zero-finding problem into a fixed point problem without any differentiability assumption.

Positive matrix eigenvector from simplex normalization

Words: 58
Brouwer fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
For a strictly positive real matrix A, the map x↦Ax/∑i​(Ax)i​ is a continuous self-map of the probability simplex. A Brouwer fixed-point theorem fixed point satisfies Ax=λx with λ>0. The image lies in the interior of the simplex, so every entry of this eigenvector is strictly positive. Nonnegative entries and nonzero columns alone do not imply this strict conclusion.

Surjectivity of a continuous bounded-displacement map

Words: 36
Brouwer fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
If a continuous map g:Rn→Rn has ∥g(x)−x∥≤K, then it is onto. For a target y, choose R≥K+∥y∥, R>0, and map the unit ball to itself by f(x)=x−(g(Rx)−y)/R. A fixed point gives g(Rx)=y.

Brouwer inward-pointing zero lemma

Words: 47
Brouwer fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let F:V→V be continuous. If ⟨F(x),x⟩<0 on the sphere ∥x∥=R, then F has a zero in the open ball. Otherwise the radial projection of F gives a map of the ball that contradicts the Brouwer fixed-point theorem.

If a polynomial equation can be rearranged as z=F(z) with a continuous F mapping a closed disk into itself, Brouwer's theorem guarantees a root in that disk.

Brouwer fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
If each component of a continuous map on a box has opposite weak signs on the corresponding pair of faces, the map has a zero.

Clamped-map proof of planar path crossing

Words: 27
Poincaré-Miranda theorem OurBigBook.com
Projecting a sign-corrected displacement map back to a square turns Brouwer's fixed point into a zero of the displacement, proving that paths joining opposite side pairs intersect.

Sperner's lemma

Words: 77
Brouwer fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
Triangulate a triangle and label every vertex by 1, 2, or 3, forbidding label i on the side opposite vertex i. Then the number of small triangles carrying all three labels is odd, and in particular at least one such triangle exists. Counting edges whose endpoint labels are 1 and 2 proves the parity statement: boundary incidences are odd, while a small triangle has odd incidence exactly when it has all three labels.

No-retraction theorem

Words: 21
Topological analysis OurBigBook.com
No closed disc retracts continuously onto its boundary. This is equivalent to Brouwer fixed-point theorem by the standard ray construction and the antipodal map.

Metric space ((X,d))

Words: 8k Articles: 136
Topological analysis OurBigBook.com
A metric space is a set X together with a metric d measuring how far apart its elements are. The elements can be positions, functions, or other objects: what matters is that the metric obeys the same basic rules. This lets one discuss convergence in a metric space, continuous maps, and Cauchy sequences without first assigning Cartesian coordinates. The useful abstraction is that many arguments require only comparisons of distances, rather than the particular objects being compared.
Even the same set can support several informative metrics. On the plane R2 with Cartesian coordinates, write x=(x1​,x2​) and y=(y1​,y2​). Three standard choices are Manhattan distance, Euclidean distance, and Chebyshev distance:
d1​(x,y)d2​(x,y)d∞​(x,y)​=∣x1​−y1​∣+∣x2​−y2​∣,=(x1​−y1​)2+(x2​−y2​)2​,=max{∣x1​−y1​∣,∣x2​−y2​∣}.​
(5)
They come from the L1 norm, Euclidean norm, and maximum norm, respectively, through d(x,y)=∥x−y∥. For O=(0,0) and P=(3,4), Manhattan distance is 3+4=7, Euclidean distance is 9+16​=5, and Chebyshev distance is max{3,4}=4. All three answers are correct for their respective metrics.
The choice encodes the question being asked. Manhattan distance models travel along a rectangular street grid. Euclidean distance measures unrestricted travel along a line segment. Chebyshev distance measures the time needed when two Cartesian coordinates can change simultaneously, each at speed at most one. Thus choosing a metric is part of modelling, rather than a consequence of knowing the endpoints. These examples have the same metric topology, but different metric path lengths and different collections of metric geodesics.
A historical reference for the general study of metric spaces is Maurice Fréchet's 1906 paper Sur quelques points du calcul fonctionnel, published in volume 22 of the Rendiconti del Circolo Matematico di Palermo. [ref]

Star metric centered at a point

Words: 136
Metric space OurBigBook.com
Given a metric space (X,d) and a∈X, define a new metric by da​(x,x)=0 and da​(x,y)=d(x,a)+d(a,y) for distinct points. It is the distance obtained by joining every point to a central vertex with its original distance to a as edge length. Symmetry and positive definiteness are immediate. With three distinct points the triangle inequality follows from the extra nonnegative term 2d(z,a) in the route through an intermediate point; repeated-point cases are immediate.
Every b=a is isolated, since Bda​​(b,d(b,a))={b}. At the centre, however, Bda​​(a,r)=Bd​(a,r). Thus a map out of this space is continuous exactly when it is continuous at a in the original metric. The closure of B is B together with a if a∈/B and d(a,B)=0; otherwise it is simply B. This construction isolates every point except the centre while preserving exactly its original neighbourhood filter.

Fixed point theorem for a strictly distance-decreasing map on a compact metric space

Words: 75
Metric space OurBigBook.com
Let X be a nonempty compact metric space and let f:X→X satisfy d(f(x),f(y))<d(x,y) whenever x=y. Then f has exactly one fixed point. The distance condition implies continuity, and x↦d(f(x),x) attains a minimum by compactness. If a minimizer p were not a fixed point, then d(f2(p),f(p))<d(f(p),p) would contradict minimality. Two distinct fixed points would contradict the same strict distance inequality directly. A uniform Lipschitz constant below 1 is unnecessary; compactness replaces the quantitative hypothesis of the contraction mapping theorem.

Product metric (d((x1​,x2​),(y1​,y2​))=d1​(x1​,y1​)+d2​(x2​,y2​))

Words: 255 Articles: 2
Metric space OurBigBook.com
For metric spaces (X1​,d1​) and (X2​,d2​), the sum metric on X1​×X2​ is the displayed formula. Nonnegativity, symmetry and the triangle inequality follow by adding the respective inequalities in the two factors, and zero distance forces equality in both coordinates. It induces the finite product topology, as does the maximum product metric, since their distances satisfy dmax​≤dsum​≤2dmax​. A sequence converges for this metric exactly when both coordinate sequences converge. Two successive extractions of a convergent subsequence therefore show that the product of two sequentially compact spaces is sequentially compact.

Countable product metric (D(x,y)=∑i≥1​2−i1+di​(xi​,yi​)di​(xi​,yi​)​)

Words: 176 Articles: 1
Product metric OurBigBook.com
The displayed metric on a countable Cartesian product of metric spaces combines the bounded metric transform with summable positive weights. It is finite even when individual factor metrics are unbounded. The triangle inequality follows from subadditivity of t/(1+t) and summation. Zero distance forces equality in each coordinate.
Convergence in this metric is exactly coordinatewise convergence. One term is bounded by the sum, so D(x(n),x)→0 implies each di​(xi(n)​,xi​)→0. Conversely, choose a finite head whose omitted weight sum is small; convergence in those finitely many coordinates controls the head uniformly, while boundedness of the transformed distances controls the entire tail. Thus it induces the countable product topology. Arbitrary positive summable weights work by the same proof.
Completeness of a countable product metric
Words: 70
Countable product metric OurBigBook.com
If every factor is a complete metric space, the countable product metric is complete. For a product-Cauchy sequence, the inequality 2−iϕ(di​(xi(m)​,xi(n)​))≤D(x(m),x(n)), with ϕ(t)=t/(1+t), makes each coordinate sequence Cauchy. Its coordinate limits define a product point. Coordinatewise convergence and the uniformly small summable tail imply convergence to that point in D. It matters that the original distances are bounded before they are summed: summing arbitrary unbounded metrics directly need not be finite.

Distortion (mathematics)

Words: 52
Metric space OurBigBook.com
Distortion measures how a mapping changes distances or geometric quantities relative to their original values. For an injective map between metric spaces, one multiplicative measure is the product of its Lipschitz constant and the Lipschitz constant of its inverse on the image. Subgroup distortion instead compares intrinsic and ambient word metrics through a growth function.

Ball (mathematics, Bd​(a,r))

Words: 172
Metric space OurBigBook.com
In a metric space (X,d), an open ball of radius r>0 about a is Bd​(a,r)={x∈X:d(a,x)<r}. A closed ball instead uses d(a,x)≤r. The strict inequality matters: a point at distance exactly r belongs to the closed ball and is excluded from the open ball. In particular, (1,0) is excluded from all three open unit balls above, and included in all three closed unit balls.
The three closed unit balls centred at zero are ∣x1​∣+∣x2​∣≤1, x12​+x22​≤1, and max{∣x1​∣,∣x2​∣}≤1. Their shapes are a diamond (a rotated square), a disk with a circle as its boundary, and an axis-aligned square. A ball need not look round! The corresponding open balls are the interiors of these shapes. At (0.8,0.8), Manhattan distance from zero is 1.6 and Euclidean distance is 1.28​≈1.131, whereas Chebyshev distance is 0.8: only the square's open unit ball contains this point.
These shapes illustrate B1​(0,1)⊆B2​(0,1)⊆B∞​(0,1), with either the open ball or closed ball convention used consistently. Their outlines are included in the displayed closed balls. In an arbitrary metric space, however, points at distance exactly r need not form the topological boundary; the discrete metric below shows why this distinction matters.

Maximum product metric (D((x,x′),(y,y′))=max{d(x,y),d′(x′,y′)})

Words: 86 Articles: 1
Metric space OurBigBook.com
The displayed metric on a product of two metric spaces satisfies its triangle inequality because max{a+c,b+d}≤max{a,b}+max{c,d} for nonnegative coordinates. Its open balls are products of equal-radius balls, so it induces the product topology.

Closed diagonal of a metric space (Δ={(x,x):x∈X})

Words: 58
Maximum product metric OurBigBook.com
For a metric space with the same metric on both factors, the diagonal is a closed subset of its product. At an off-diagonal point (x,y) let δ=d(x,y)>0. A maximum-metric ball of radius δ/3 misses the diagonal, since a common coordinate z would give d(x,y)≤d(x,z)+d(z,y)<2δ/3. Equality of underlying sets without equality or compatibility of the metrics is a different assertion.

Metric epsilon-net (ε-net)

Words: 56
Metric space OurBigBook.com
An epsilon-net in a metric space is a set within distance ε of every point. A maximal ε-separated set is an epsilon-net: any uncovered point could be added. On the unit sphere of Rk, disjoint Euclidean balls of radius ε/2 around separated points lie in the ball of radius 1+ε/2. Comparing Lebesgue measures gives a net of cardinality at most (1+2/ε)k.

Uniform metric (d∞​(f,g)=supx​d(f(x),g(x)))

Words: 98 Articles: 1
Metric space OurBigBook.com
The supremum of pointwise distances defines a metric on maps when it is finite, for example if the target metric space is bounded. Convergence in this metric is uniform convergence. If the target is complete, Cauchy sequences have pointwise limits and the Cauchy estimate makes convergence uniform.

Completeness of the continuous-map space in the uniform metric (C(X,Y) is complete when Y is complete and bounded)

Words: 54
Uniform metric OurBigBook.com
A Cauchy sequence in the uniform metric has a pointwise limit in the complete target, and the common Cauchy bound makes convergence uniform. The triangle inequality with one fixed continuous approximant shows that the limit is continuous. Thus the space of all continuous maps into a bounded complete metric space is complete, with no compactness assumption on the domain.

Separated subset of a metric space (d(x,y)≥r(x=y))

Words: 135 Articles: 2
Metric space OurBigBook.com
A subset is r-separated if distinct points have distance at least r. Such a subset is a packing by points; small balls around them have disjoint interiors at suitable radius. A large separated set supplies many distinguishable alternatives in statistical lower-bound arguments.

Inclusion-maximal separated set

Words: 93 Articles: 1
Separated subset of a metric space OurBigBook.com
An inclusion-maximal separated set is one to which no further point of the ambient metric space can be added while keeping the same separation. It need not have the largest possible cardinality. In a finite space it can be obtained by repeatedly adding an admissible point.
Maximal separated sets give covers
Words: 51
Inclusion-maximal separated set OurBigBook.com
If an inclusion-maximal separated set has separation at least r, every point of the ambient metric space is at distance strictly less than r from a selected point. Metric space OurBigBook.com
The metric topology consists of the sets U such that, for every x∈U, some open ball Bd​(x,r) lies in U. Thus open sets describe which sufficiently small changes remain inside a region; they do not specify the numerical size of those changes.
For v∈R2, the L1 norm, Euclidean norm, and maximum norm satisfy
∥v∥∞​≤∥v∥2​≤∥v∥1​≤2​∥v∥2​≤2∥v∥∞​.

These bounds make them equivalent norms. For example, B∞​(a,r/2)⊆B1​(a,r)⊆B∞​(a,r): every open ball contains a sufficiently small open ball for either other metric. Hence all three define the same open sets, convergent sequences, and continuous maps. More generally, any two norms on a real or complex finite-dimensional vector space are equivalent norms; see H. A. Priestley, Functional Analysis I, §§0.5–0.7 and Theorem 4.3.
The metric topology therefore does not determine numerical distances. Multiplying a metric by 100 preserves its open sets while multiplying every distance by 100. Nor does the general equivalence of metrics require constant-factor bounds: that stronger comparison holds for the three norms used here.

Metric (d)

Words: 502 Articles: 9
Metric space OurBigBook.com
A metric on a set X is a function d:X×X→[0,∞) satisfying, for every x,y,z∈X:
  • d(x,y)≥0: distances are nonnegative and finite.
  • d(x,y)=0 if and only if x=y: distinct elements have positive distance.
  • d(x,y)=d(y,x): exchanging the endpoints leaves the distance unchanged.
  • d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z): the triangle inequality.
A metric equips its underlying set with a metric space structure; the distance function and the space carrying it are distinct concepts. The second requirement distinguishes a metric from a pseudometric, which may identify distinct elements at zero distance. The symmetry requirement also explains why directed travel times, such as uphill versus downhill times, need not define a metric.
A tempting alternative on the real numbers is d(x,y)=(x−y)2. It is nonnegative, symmetric, and zero exactly on equal endpoints, but fails the triangle inequality: d(0,2)=4>1+1=d(0,1)+d(1,2). Checking only the first three requirements would miss the failure.

Every nonempty set equipped with the discrete metric is a bounded set, even if it is an infinite set. For 0<r<1, both the open ball and closed ball about a are the singleton {a}. At r=1, the open ball is still {a}, but the closed ball is the whole space; for r>1, both are the whole space. Every subset is both an open set and a closed set. Consequently the boundary of the radius-one closed ball is empty, even though every point other than a is at distance exactly one. Take O=(0,0), Q=(3,0), and P=(3,4). For Euclidean distance, the triangle inequality reads 5≤3+4=7. The direct line segment has metric path length 5, while the route through Q has metric path length 7. For Manhattan distance, the same comparison becomes 7=3+4: both routes are shortest. The line segment and the bent route both become metric geodesics when progress is measured by metric path length. For a nonempty subset F of a metric space, the distance to a set is d(x,F)=infy∈F​d(x,y). The triangle inequality gives d(x,F)≤d(x,z)+d(z,F); swapping x,z proves ∣d(x,F)−d(z,F)∣≤d(x,z). Thus it is one-Lipschitz. Its zero set is exactly the closure of F: every neighbourhood of x meets F precisely when this infimum vanishes. For a closed set, zero distance therefore implies membership. When the empty set is allowed, use the convention d(x,∅)=+∞; the finite-valued Lipschitz assertion applies to nonempty sets.

Two nonempty disjoint compact sets have positive set distance: continuity attains the minimum on their Cartesian product, and a zero minimum would give a common point. Thus the non-isolated points of X×Y are (X′×Y)∪(X×Y′), where the primes denote the non-isolated points in the spaces themselves.

It defines a pseudometric on the Cauchy sequences, and its metric quotient identifies sequences whose mutual distance tends to zero. Constant sequences embed the original metric space isometrically. Their image is dense, because the class of (xn​) is approached by the constant classes of xn​. The quotient is complete: from a Cauchy sequence of its points select a subsequence whose successive distances are below 2−j and choose original-space points within 2−j of these subsequence points. Those original-space points form a Cauchy sequence and its class is the limit of the subsequence, hence of the whole sequence. Words: 270
Baire category theorem OurBigBook.com
If an entire function f is not a polynomial, then there is a point z0​∈C for which f(n)(z0​)=0 for every nonnegative integer n. Consequently every coefficient in the Taylor series of f about z0​ is nonzero.
For each n, the function f(n) is not identically zero, since otherwise f would be a polynomial. Its zero set is closed and has empty interior by the identity theorem, hence is a nowhere dense set. The Baire category theorem says that the complete metric space C cannot be the union of these countably many zero sets.
Set Sn​={x:f(n)(x)=0} and En​=intSn​. The sets Sn​ are closed, En​⊂En+1​, and Baire's theorem on each interval shows that Ω=⋃n​En​ is dense. On every connected component of Ω, compactness and the increasing cover by the En​ show that one derivative vanishes locally with a uniform finite order, so f agrees there with one polynomial.
If F=R∖Ω were nonempty, it would be closed and have no isolated points: polynomial pieces on both sides of an isolated point would have matching derivatives of every order and hence join into one polynomial piece. Applying Baire's theorem to the cover F=⋃n​(F∩Sn​) gives an interval U and an index k for which F∩U is nonempty and contained in Sk​. Because F has no isolated points, difference quotients show that every derivative of order at least k vanishes on F∩U. Each polynomial component of Ω meeting U has an endpoint in F∩U, so its degree is less than k. Thus f(k)=0 throughout U, contradicting F∩U=∅. Hence Ω=R, and its sole connected component carries one polynomial.

For a Cauchy sequence (Fn​) of these sets, define An​=⋃m≥n​Fm​​ and δn​=supp,q≥n​dH​(Fp​,Fq​). A Cauchy sequence in any metric space is bounded, so its tail sets are contained in a common finite-radius neighbourhood of one bounded FN​; hence every An​ is bounded.
